| ID | Kind | Role |
|---|---|---|

| `sm-admin-write-path` | entrypoint | `admin.py update_value` — internal write path, no instrumentation |

| `sm-storage-layer` | service | whole-file read/rewrite over the flat file |

| `sm-evictor-scheduler` | job | assumed caller of the pass; not in this repo |

payload_or_id.title: Synchronised TTL expiry drives periodic bursts of whole-file reads
payload_or_id.description: Introduced by the evictor fix. While eviction was inoperative the cache absorbed every key after its first read and storage read load fell to near zero. Now entries genuinely expire, and because inserted_at_ms is set at insertion, keys first requested together expire together: the working set drains in a batch one TTL after it was loaded, and the next request for each key is a miss. Every miss is a full O(dataset) read_text of the flat file, so the service sees a synchronised burst of whole-file reads once per TTL rather than a smooth trickle. There is no jitter on the TTL, no request coalescing, and no single-flight guard, so N concurrent misses on the same key produce N independent full-file reads. The steady-state storage read load of this service is strictly higher after the fix than before it.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass has no caller in this repository; the scheduler loop is assumed to exist outside it. If that loop is not deployed, is misconfigured, crashes, or is paused, eviction stops entirely. Promoted to critical at this revision: with the unit mismatch fixed, this and fm-evictor-pass-crash-concurrent-mutation are the only two remaining ways eviction can stop, so this entry now occupies the structural position that justified rating the unit mismatch critical -- it does not self-heal, and it removes both the cache's memory bound and its staleness ceiling at once, terminating in fm-process-oom and in unbounded fm-stale-read-served. Its observable effect is identical to a crashed pass, which is why the two must be distinguished by instrumentation rather than inferred from cache size alone.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass crashes on concurrent cache mutation
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass builds its expired-key list by iterating cache.items(), which is a live ItemsView over the Cache's dict rather than a snapshot. A request thread completing a cache miss inserts into that dict during the walk, raising RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. The pass dies mid-walk, having evicted nothing, since eviction happens only after the comprehension completes. Untouched by the evictor fix and live today. Promoted to critical at this revision for the same reason as fm-evictor-scheduler-absent: it is now one of only two ways eviction stops. It is also more likely to fire after the fix than before, because fm-cache-expiry-stampede means misses -- and therefore dict insertions -- now arrive in synchronised bursts timed to the same TTL boundary the eviction pass walks. Whether a crashed pass is ever retried is decided by the unimplemented scheduler, so under sustained miss traffic this can be permanently fatal to eviction rather than transient.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass result is discarded
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the number of entries removed explicitly so a caller can observe progress, but nothing in this repository records it and the pass emits no metric or log of its own. The fix to the unit comparison changes what this blindness costs rather than removing it. Before the fix a working pass and a broken one both returned 0, so the defect hid in a constant. After the fix a return of 0 is a legitimate reading -- it means nothing was past TTL -- so a pass that is running correctly against a young cache, a pass that is crashing on concurrent mutation before it evicts anything, and a pass that is never invoked at all remain mutually indistinguishable from outside. This is the reason fm-evictor-scheduler-absent and fm-evictor-pass-crash-concurrent-mutation can persist silently, rather than an independent runtime fault.

payload_or_id.title: Absent-key lookups are cached as negative entries
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a miss unconditionally, including a None returned for a key not present in storage. The negative entry is indistinguishable from a real cached value and is subject to the same expiry rules. With eviction working, a key looked up before it is first written is pinned to 'absent' for up to one TTL rather than for the process lifetime, so the condition now self-heals; while eviction is stopped it reverts to permanent. Negative entries also consume the same heap as real ones, so lookups of keys that do not exist -- scans and scrapers in particular -- still feed fm-cache-unbounded-growth.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Structural property of the code rather than a runtime condition: Cache.get caches None unconditionally on every miss, so the property is true on every request including every healthy one. No threshold over it separates healthy from unhealthy -- a rule written on it would fire constantly or never. It is detected through its consequence, fm-new-key-never-visible, which does have a runtime signal and is covered by KvstoreNegativeCacheDominant and KvstoreAbsentReadsSpike. The correct remediation is a code change -- do not cache negatives, or give them a shorter TTL than positives -- not a rule and not a metric. Correction: an earlier revision of this reason said the negative-entry share 'belongs as a label on the recommended cache-entry metric', and that wording was wrong in a way that mattered. It conflated quantifying a property with detecting it, and the resulting link from mr-cache-entries to this mode was rejected as coverage of an excluded failure mode. The entry_kind label on kvstore_cache_entries is retained, but purely as diagnostic context for the cache-growth alert; it is not coverage of this entry, and this entry carries no metric or alert coverage by design. The evictor fix does not disturb this exclusion: bounding the lifetime of a negative entry changes how long the property persists, not whether it is a property of every request.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Cache holds a dict entry per distinct key ever requested, with no size cap and no LRU. The evictor fix gives it a bound it did not previously have, but the bound is the set of distinct keys seen within one TTL window, not a memory figure: sustained unique-key traffic -- scans, scrapers, and lookups of keys that do not exist -- can still exceed the host's memory inside a single 300s window, because nothing caps entry count or bytes. The fix therefore narrows this mode from unconditional to rate-dependent rather than eliminating it, and it reverts to fully unbounded whenever eviction stops for either of the two remaining reasons.

payload_or_id.title: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value accepts cache as a parameter, writes through to Storage.put, and never calls cache.evict(key). Cache.get returns any already-cached entry without re-consulting storage, so a write is invisible to readers holding that key in this process. Downgraded to warning at this revision: the divergence it opens is now closed by the evictor within one TTL instead of never, so it self-heals. The defect itself is untouched -- cache.evict remains uncalled by any writer, and the correct fix is still one line in admin.update_value -- but its consequence is bounded staleness rather than permanent staleness, which is a ticket rather than a page.

payload_or_id.title: Reader is served a stale value for up to one TTL after a write
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value for a key that was cached before a write and receives the pre-write value. get_value increments outcome=success and returns normally, so the failure stays silent at every layer: correct-looking response, healthy-looking metric, wrong data. Downgraded from critical to warning at this revision. Staleness was previously unbounded -- no writer invalidated and no evictor expired, so a stale value persisted for the process lifetime. With eviction working the window is bounded by TTL_SECONDS plus the scheduler interval, roughly five minutes, and it closes on its own. That is ordinary TTL-cache behaviour rather than a paging condition. The upstream causes that restore unboundedness are retained: if eviction stops for either remaining reason, or if writes are failing or being lost, the ceiling disappears and this reverts to a permanent wrong answer.

payload_or_id.title: Newly written key stays invisible to readers that looked it up early
payload_or_id.description: A key looked up before it exists caches None; when the sync job later writes it, no invalidation occurs, so get_value keeps returning None until the negative entry expires. A transient absence of the backing file poisons this way in bulk -- every key requested during that window is pinned to 'absent' -- and the poisoning outlives the outage that caused it. Downgraded from critical to warning at this revision for the same reason as fm-stale-read-served: the evictor now clears negative entries within one TTL, so both the single-key case and the bulk-poisoning case self-heal in roughly five minutes instead of persisting for the process lifetime. Distinct from fm-stale-read-served because the client sees 'no such key' rather than an outdated value, which is the harder of the two for a client to distinguish from a legitimate answer. Reverts to permanent whenever eviction stops.

payload_or_id.title: Storage read fails and raises StorageError
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get catches OSError from read_text and re-raises it as StorageError. Cache.get does not catch it, so it propagates through the cache to the entrypoint on every cache miss. The evictor fix materially enlarges the blast radius of this mode. Previously only uncached keys were affected and cached keys were served from memory indefinitely, so a total loss of the backing file produced a partial, key-dependent error rate that never grew. Now every entry expires within one TTL and every subsequent read is a miss, so the same storage outage escalates from partial to total within roughly five minutes. The cache no longer masks a storage failure, it only delays it. The upside for detection is that the error rate ramps over a TTL rather than sitting at a constant partial level, which is a clearer signal than the flat one it replaced. Alertable today via the existing counter's outcome=error label, though that label cannot attribute the error to storage specifically.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file absent is silently treated as an empty store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get returns None when the path does not exist rather than raising. A deleted file, an unmounted volume, a wrong path in configuration, or a mount that is not ready at process start are all reported to callers as 'this key has no value'. No exception is raised, so get_value increments outcome=success and the one existing metric reads as healthy while the entire dataset is unreadable. As with fm-storage-read-error, the evictor fix enlarges the blast radius: cached keys previously continued to be served correctly through the outage, whereas now every key reads as absent within one TTL of the file disappearing. This is the more dangerous of the two escalations, because the failure it escalates into is silent -- a total outage that presents as a fully successful, fully empty store.

payload_or_id.title: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: A cache miss reading the file while put is rewriting it sees a truncated or partly written snapshot, since nothing serialises the two. The reader returns None for keys not in the fragment it read, or a partial final line as a value. The result is then cached, so a microsecond-wide race is still converted into a persistent wrong answer -- now bounded to one TTL rather than to the process lifetime. The evictor fix reduces the duration of each instance while increasing the number of instances: fm-cache-expiry-stampede means misses now arrive in synchronised bursts, so there are far more reads competing with any given rewrite than there were when the cache absorbed everything permanently.

payload_or_id.title: Client receives a value belonging to a different key
payload_or_id.description: The terminal link of the format chain: get_value returns a syntactically valid value that belongs to another key or to a fragment of one. This is the worst-shaped failure in the service -- the response is well-formed, the request is counted as a success, and the wrong value is cached. Unaffected by the evictor fix in its two format-defect forms: fm-key-comma-collision and fm-value-newline-corruption corrupt the flat file itself, so expiry and re-read return the same wrong value, and the contamination is permanent regardless of cache lifetime. Only the fm-partial-read-during-rewrite path is now self-healing, because that one corrupts the cache without corrupting the file. Remains critical on the strength of the two that are not.

payload_or_id.title: Client-visible read latency degrades
payload_or_id.description: The terminal link of the performance chain: cache misses become progressively slower as the dataset grows, and after the evictor fix misses are both far more frequent and clustered. Clients observe rising tail latency, periodic latency spikes at TTL boundaries, and eventually timeouts. The existing counter records outcome only, never duration, so this is invisible at the entrypoint until it becomes severe enough to show up as client-side timeouts. The service's own steady-state read amplification is now higher than it was at the previously analysed revision, which makes fm-storage-scan-latency-growth bite sooner at any given dataset size.

| ID | Definition site | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| `mx-get-value-requests-total` | `kvstore/api.py:19-23` | `Counter`, one label `outcome`, two series. Call sites `api.py:30` (error) and `api.py:32` (success). |
| `mx-prometheus-default-collectors` | *none in this repo* | `process_*`/`python_gc_*`, registered as a side effect of importing `prometheus_client`. Not instrumentation this service chose. |

Both had an empty `emitted_at`; I've tied the real metric to its definition site. The service defines no `Gauge`, `Histogram` or `Summary`, constructs no registry, and calls neither `start_http_server` nor `make_wsgi_app` — so `fm-metrics-never-exposed` still gates everything below it.

**Coverage status across 27 failure modes:** 4 `alertable`, 2 `excluded`, 21 `metric-gap`. One metric covering one of ~19 distinct fault paths.

**The most important finding of this phase: the fix upgrades a metric recommendation's power.** `mr-cache-oldest-entry-age` was previously a weak trend signal — under the unit mismatch it grew without limit on *every* deployment, healthy-looking or not, so there was no threshold that meant anything. Now the code guarantees no entry outlives `TTL_SECONDS`, which turns the gauge into an **invariant check**: a sustained reading above TTL + one scheduler interval is direct proof eviction has stopped, catches either remaining cause, and fires long before memory pressure appears. annotations.summary: kvstore cache misses are arriving in synchronised bursts rather than a steady rate
annotations.description: Peak miss rate over the last 30 minutes is more than five times the average, with the peak high enough to matter in absolute terms. This is the signature of synchronised TTL expiry: Entry.inserted_at_ms is stamped at insertion and TTL_SECONDS is a fixed 300 with no jitter, so keys loaded together expire together and the next request for each is a miss. Every miss is a full O(dataset) read_text of the backing file, and there is no request coalescing or single-flight guard, so N concurrent misses on the same key issue N independent whole-file reads. Note this condition did not exist at the previously analysed revision -- while eviction was inoperative the cache absorbed each key permanently after its first read, so steady-state storage load is strictly higher now than it was before the evictor was fixed. Corroborate with kvstore_eviction_entries_removed_total arriving in large periodic batches and with kvstore_storage_operation_duration_seconds spiking at the same boundaries. The remedy is a code change -- add jitter to the per-entry TTL and coalesce concurrent misses on the same key -- not a threshold adjustment.

annotations.summary: kvstore cached entries are far older than TTL_SECONDS
annotations.description: The oldest cached entry is more than three times TTL_SECONDS (300). Repointed at this revision, and materially stronger than it was. Previously the ms/s unit mismatch meant entry age grew without limit on every deployment, healthy or not, so no threshold over it carried information. The fixed evictor now guarantees that no entry outlives TTL, which makes this an invariant check rather than a trend: a sustained reading above TTL plus one scheduler interval is direct evidence that eviction has stopped, and it catches either remaining cause -- a scheduler that is not running, or a pass that is crashing mid-walk -- without needing to know which. It fires well before cache growth threatens memory, making it the earliest reliable detector in both the staleness chain and the memory chain. Remains a proxy by necessity: a stale read is byte-for-byte identical to a correct one and increments outcome=success, so no entrypoint metric can detect the failure directly. It does not prove any client received stale data, only that nothing is bounding how wrong an answer could be. Critical because the two eviction-stopper modes it serves are critical, even though fm-stale-read-served alone is now a warning.

annotations.summary: kvstore eviction passes complete but remove nothing while entries are past TTL
annotations.description: Passes are running to completion and removing zero entries even though the oldest cached entry is well past TTL_SECONDS (300). Repointed and downgraded at this revision. It previously detected the ms/s unit mismatch in run_eviction_pass and was the highest-value rule in this set; that defect is fixed at this SHA, so the rule is now a regression guard against the expiry comparison silently ceasing to match rather than a detector of a live fault. It is kept rather than deleted because the bug it caught was invisible for exactly as long as it existed -- the pass reported success and returned 0 throughout -- and this rule plus the recorded removal count is the only thing that would have caught it. It serves fm-evictor-result-unrecorded, which is the standing blindness that let the original defect persist: the pass's only output is still discarded today. The third conjunct is load-bearing, not decoration -- zero removals is perfectly correct when nothing is old enough, so without the age precondition this fires on every healthy idle service. Severity is warning because both modes it now serves are warnings; if it fires alongside KvstoreCacheStalenessCeilingExceeded, treat that critical as the actionable one.

annotations.summary: kvstore eviction pass has not completed recently
annotations.description: No successful eviction pass within the threshold window. The scheduler loop that calls run_eviction_pass is not implemented in this repository, so it may be undeployed, misconfigured, paused or dead. Raised from warning to critical at this revision: with the ms/s unit mismatch fixed, a dead scheduler is now one of only two remaining ways eviction can stop, so this rule went from partly redundant -- eviction was already inoperative for another reason -- to load-bearing. While it holds, the cache has no memory bound and cached values have no staleness ceiling, and neither condition self-heals. The 900s threshold is a placeholder: set it to a small multiple of the deployed scheduler's actual interval, which is not discoverable from this code. Written on a timestamp rather than a counter rate because absence of increase is not a value a threshold rule can fire on.

annotations.summary: kvstore eviction passes are raising exceptions
annotations.description: run_eviction_pass is dying mid-walk. The expected cause is RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration -- the pass iterates cache.items(), a live view over the Cache's dict rather than a snapshot, so a concurrent request completing a cache miss mutates it during the walk. Raised from warning to critical at this revision: this defect was untouched by the evictor fix and is now one of only two remaining ways eviction stops. It is also more likely to fire than before, because synchronised TTL expiry clusters cache-miss insertions at the same boundary the pass walks -- see KvstoreCacheExpiryStampede. A crashing pass evicts nothing at all, since removal happens only after the comprehension completes, and whether it is ever retried is decided by the unimplemented scheduler. Distinguishing this from a dead scheduler is exactly why passes are counted with an outcome label: both otherwise present as 'nothing is being evicted' but need different fixes -- snapshot the keys before walking, versus repair the scheduler.

annotations.summary: kvstore cache floor is high and still rising
annotations.description: Rewritten at this revision to survive the sawtooth the evictor fix introduces. Entry count now oscillates by design -- rising as misses insert and dropping as each pass clears a batch -- so a rule written on the instantaneous value would page on healthy operation. This tests the trough instead: the minimum over a full hour, spanning roughly twelve TTL cycles, is above the expected working set and the hour-scale trend is still upward. That is growth eviction is failing to reclaim, as opposed to the normal cycle. The fix bounds the cache to the distinct keys seen within one TTL window rather than to a memory figure, so sustained unique-key traffic from scans, scrapers, or lookups of nonexistent keys can still exhaust memory inside a single window. Fires hours to days before the process is OOM-killed, which is the point of alerting on the cause rather than the terminal symptom. The 100000 threshold is a placeholder: set it from the observed steady-state working set, since a service with a genuinely large key space is not failing merely by being large.

annotations.summary: kvstore resident memory is high or trending toward the limit
annotations.description: Resident memory is above the threshold, or linear extrapolation of the last hour puts it above within four hours. The rationale changed at this revision: with the evictor working, memory no longer climbs monotonically on every deployment, so a sustained upward trend is now genuinely anomalous rather than the expected steady state. That makes predict_linear meaningful here where it previously described normal behaviour. A trend that does not flatten means unique-key arrival within each TTL window exceeds what eviction reclaims, or eviction has stopped -- check KvstoreCacheStalenessCeilingExceeded to separate the two. Uses process_resident_memory_bytes, which prometheus_client registers automatically, so no code change is needed; but it is Linux-only and cannot attribute growth to the cache, which is why kvstore_cache_entries is the better primary signal. Set 3e9 to the container's actual memory limit; it is a placeholder, not a measured value.

annotations.summary: Most of the kvstore cache is negative entries
annotations.description: Negative entries dominate the cache. Cache.get stores None unconditionally on a miss, so every key looked up before it was first written is pinned to 'absent' until that entry expires. Downgraded from critical to warning at this revision: with eviction working these entries now clear within one TTL, so both the single-key case and bulk poisoning from a storage outage self-heal in roughly five minutes rather than persisting for the process lifetime, and a restart is no longer required to clear the damage. The 30m for-duration is what makes it still worth alerting on -- a condition that ought to drain within one TTL but has held for six consecutive TTLs means either the absent-key traffic is genuinely dominant or eviction has stopped, and KvstoreCacheStalenessCeilingExceeded separates those. Distinct from KvstoreAbsentReadsSpike, which sees the symptom in traffic; this sees the poisoned state itself.

annotations.description: Writes are landing in storage while zero writer-sourced invalidations occur, the direct signature of admin.update_value never calling cache.evict. Downgraded from critical to warning at this revision: the defect is untouched -- no writer calls evict, and the fix is still one line -- but its consequence is now bounded staleness rather than permanent divergence, because the working evictor closes the window within one TTL. A key written while cached is wrong for up to five minutes instead of forever, which is a ticket rather than a page. The 'or vector(0)' is required rather than cosmetic: a label value that has never been observed produces no series at all, so a bare comparison would return empty and the rule would never fire -- which is precisely the case when the bug is present. Still worth alerting on because it detects the defect at the write, rather than waiting for a user to notice wrong data.

annotations.summary: kvstore get_value is failing for more than 1% of requests
annotations.description: get_value is re-raising StorageError to clients. StorageError has exactly one source in this service -- an OSError from reading the backing file -- so this indicates the filesystem or the file itself is unavailable. The evictor fix changes how this presents, and for the better: previously only cache misses reached storage and already-cached keys kept succeeding indefinitely, so a total filesystem failure showed up as a flat, partial, key-dependent error rate that never grew. Now every entry expires within one TTL and every subsequent read is a miss, so the same outage escalates from partial to total within roughly five minutes. Expect a ramp rather than a step, and do not read a low initial rate as a small problem -- the cache is delaying the failure, not containing it. This is the one alert in this set that needs no new instrumentation.

annotations.summary: kvstore backing file is missing -- reads are silently returning empty
annotations.description: Storage.get took its not-exists branch, returning None rather than raising. This is the most dangerous silent failure in the service: a deleted file, unmounted volume or misconfigured path is reported to clients as 'this key has no value' and counted as outcome=success, so without this rule every dashboard reads as perfectly healthy while the entire dataset is unreadable. The evictor fix widens the blast radius: cached keys previously continued to be served correctly straight through the outage, whereas now every key reads as absent within one TTL of the file disappearing, so a partial silent failure becomes a total silent failure in about five minutes. The one improvement is that the damage no longer outlives the outage -- poisoned negative entries now expire within a TTL once the file returns, so a restart is no longer needed to clear them.

annotations.summary: kvstore is returning 'no such key' for an unusually high share of requests
annotations.description: Client-boundary detection for the shared symptom of three distinct failures: the backing file is missing or truncated, or the cache is serving poisoned negative entries. After the evictor fix the signal is sharper for the storage-loss causes: because every entry now expires within one TTL, a vanished backing file drives this ratio toward 100% instead of plateauing at whatever fraction of traffic was uncached. The 20% threshold assumes lookups of genuinely absent keys are a minority of traffic; calibrate against the observed baseline.

annotations.summary: kvstore cache-miss reads are slow at p99 (> 1s)

Deliberately filtered to result=miss: with a large cache the hit rate is high enough that an unlabeled aggregate would dilute a badly degraded miss path into an acceptable-looking percentile. Calibration note for this revision: the evictor fix raises both the frequency and the clustering of misses, so the miss-path p99 is expected to sit higher than it did at the previously analysed SHA and to spike at TTL boundaries. Baseline this threshold against post-fix traffic rather than carrying over a pre-fix value, or it will page on the new normal. annotations.summary: kvstore process has restarted more than once in the last hour
annotations.description: Repeated restarts, the expected signature of an OOM kill under cache growth. The cycle is self-perpetuating: the restart discards the cache, traffic refills it, and memory climbs to the limit again on a period set by traffic volume. With the evictor working this is no longer the inevitable end state of every deployment, so repeated restarts now indicate either that unique-key arrival within a TTL window genuinely exceeds available memory or that eviction has stopped -- check KvstoreCacheStalenessCeilingExceeded and KvstoreEvictionPassCrashing. Note the request counter cannot record the kill -- the process holding it dies with it -- so the only entrypoint-side signal is a gap in data, which is why restart detection is a separate rule. Each restart also risks truncating the backing file if it lands mid-rewrite, so check kvstore_storage_records after any occurrence.

A key or value violating the flat file's implicit format constraints was written or parsed. The format has no escaping and Storage.get partitions on the first comma, so a key containing a comma collides with a different key -- a lookup of 'a' matches the line stored for 'a,b' and returns 'b,value'. A value containing a newline injects a phantom record instead. Both produce a well-formed, confidently-served wrong answer. Unaffected by the evictor fix, and this is the important distinction: these two defects corrupt the backing file itself, so expiry and re-read return the same wrong value and the contamination is permanent regardless of cache lifetime. Only the mid-rewrite-read cause, also served here, is now self-healing, because that one corrupts the cache without corrupting the file. Fires on any occurrence with no rate threshold: a single corrupt record is a correctness defect, not a level to be tolerated.
